extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians; advanced students and attendees of mathematical congresses
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for selecting, formulating, and solving significant mathematical research problems, and for judging the quality of solutions and proofs. Covers desiderata such as clarity, difficulty, significance, rigor, sources of problems, and proof strategies (generalization/specialization, impossibility proofs, axiomatization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and easy comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: „Das Klare und leicht Faßliche zieht uns an ... ein mathematisches Problem ... sollte klar und leicht faßlich sein.“ (Hilbert argues that a perfect problem should be clear and readily comprehensible.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes that a good mathematical problem ought to be presented so it can be grasped easily; clarity attracts researchers while convoluted statements repel. He invokes the maxim that a theory/problem should be made clear enough to be explained simply (even to a passer-by), and demands even more of a problem than of a theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate difficulty (challenging but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: „Ein mathematisches Problem sei ferner schwierig, damit es uns reizt, und dennoch nicht völlig unzugänglich...“
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valuable problem should be hard enough to stimulate effort and invention, yet not utterly inaccessible so as to mock attempts. It should both challenge and reward the researcher with satisfying solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific importance / significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should have „hohe Bedeutung ... für den Fortschritt der mathematischen Wissenschaft im Allgemeinen“; their value is measured by the gain to science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert stresses that important problems advance the general development of mathematics; the true worth of a problem is judged by the benefits its solution brings to the discipline (new results, methods, concepts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness: potential to generate new methods and fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Good problems often lead to the discovery of new methods and the birth of new subfields (examples: Bernoulli's brachistochrone → calculus of variations; Fermat → ideal numbers and algebraic number theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives historical examples where specific problems produced entire theories; a desirable problem is one that opens new techniques and broader perspectives beyond its original statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-disciplinary impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The same specific problem can 'eingreift' (reach into) various different branches of mathematics (e.g., shortest line problem influences geometry, mechanics, variational calculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer problems that connect multiple areas or yield analogies across disciplines; such problems increase unity and transfer of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of problems: empirical and internal (creation by pure thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems arise both from experience/outer world (mechanics, astronomy, physics) and from the independent activity of pure mathematical thought (generalizing, specializing, combining concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert recommends attention to both sources: applied/empirical phenomena supply classical problems, while internally generated questions (through logical combination and abstraction) create many finer modern problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of finite deductive proof from finite assumptions (rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: „daß es gelingt, die Richtigkeit der Antwort durch eine endliche Anzahl von Schlüssen darzuthun und zwar auf Grund einer endlichen Anzahl von Voraussetzungen, welche in der Problemstellung liegen ...“
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct solution must be demonstrated by a finite chain of logical deductions from explicitly stated (finite) hypotheses; this is the demand for mathematical rigor and the core standard for a complete solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for rigor because it fosters simplicity and fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert rejects the idea that rigor is the enemy of simplicity: rigorous methods often yield simpler, more development-capable approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor tends to force discovery of simpler, more general proofs and methods (examples: functional methods simplifying algebraic curve theory; Weierstrass' foundation of the calculus of variations). Thus proofs should aim for logical strictness as it promotes clarity and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatization and clear foundations for new concepts and notations
rubrics_metrics.description: New concepts require a system of axioms and appropriate new symbols; geometric figures and other new signs must have their axiomatic content examined before use as strict proof tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new terms and symbols by first fixing their axiomatic relations so they can be manipulated rigorously; the choice of notation should reflect the phenomena that motivated the concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diagrams/figures dependent on axiomatic grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: „Die Anwendung der geometrischen Zeichen als strenges Beweismittel setzt die genaue Kenntniß und völlige Beherrschung der Axiome voraus.“
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric drawings and visual signs are indispensable, but their use in proofs requires that the underlying axioms be known and controlled; figures must be incorporated into rigorous axiom systems before being relied upon in deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek general viewpoints (generalization) when stuck
rubrics_metrics.description: If one cannot solve a problem, often the cause is failure to recognize a more general viewpoint that makes the given problem a special case and reveals applicable methods (examples: Cauchy's complex paths, Kummer's ideal concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unifying generalizations that place the problem within a broader class where established techniques apply; this is often the most reliable path to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialize to simpler subproblems when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: „...das Specialisiren ...: einfachere und leichtere Probleme als das vorgelegte ... noch nicht oder noch unvollkommen erledigt haben ... Diese Vorschrift ist einer der wichtigsten Hebel zur Ueberwindung mathematischer Schwierigkeiten.“
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and solve simpler or related problems whose solutions and tools can be lifted to the original problem; specialization is a key practical method often used (sometimes unconsciously) by mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove impossibility when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If solution under given hypotheses is impossible, one should aim to prove that impossibility (example: classical impossibility proofs like in antiquity or impossibility of certain constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When positive resolution seems unreachable, formulate and attempt a rigorous impossibility proof under the stated assumptions; such proofs can be as scientifically valuable as existence proofs (e.g., proof of impossibility can lead to new laws in other sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical existence tied to non-contradiction (consistency of axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: „Wenn man einem Begriffe Merkmale erteilt, die einander widersprechen, so sage ich: der Begriff existirt mathematisch nicht. ... Gelingt es ... zu beweisen, daß die dem Begriffe erteilten Merkmale ... niemals zu einem Widerspruche führen können, so sage ich, daß damit die mathematische Existenz des Begriffes ... bewiesen worden ist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show that a mathematical object 'exists' in the rigorous sense, one must demonstrate that the axioms defining it are mutually consistent (no finite deduction leads to contradiction); Hilbert stresses proving consistency (e.g., of the axioms of arithmetic) as a fundamental problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems should be grafted onto established knowledge (connectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new problem is like a young shoot that thrives only if grafted onto the old trunk — i.e., it should be connected to the secure stock of existing mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate problems and proofs so they fit into and build upon the existing mathematical corpus; anchoring new questions to well-understood foundations increases their tractability and the fruitfulness of their solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a problem judged after its solution (retrospective assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: „Es ist schwierig und oft unmöglich, den Wert eines Problems im Voraus richtig zu beurteilen; denn schließlich entscheidet der Gewinn, den die Wissenschaft dem Problem verdankt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the true value of a problem often only becomes clear after its resolution; therefore selection should consider plausibility of significant payoff but accept uncertainty.
